rationale: The Shootout lists benchmark is a small, memory-bound C++ program dominated by pointer-chasing through linked lists, short functions, and moderate-count iteration loops, with negligible arithmetic intensity; this makes cheap data- and call-oriented transforms nearly free at runtime, so SUB, SPLIT, and ICALL get high weights across security and diversity dimensions and are allowed to apply broadly (high RuntimeCost/SizeCost tolerance since instruction substitution and splitting add negligible latency versus cache-miss-dominated execution). FLA receives a strong SecurityGain weight because flattening the list-traversal and merge loops yields the largest reverse-engineering payoff on this control-flow-simple workload, but its RuntimeCost and SizeCost weights are kept low so the selector restricts it to functions whose hot-loop profiles can absorb the dispatch overhead; BCF is similarly constrained (lowest RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights) since bogus predicates bloat a tiny binary and tax hot loops for limited marginal gain beyond FLA. IBR is given a moderate profile to add branch indirection on the pointer-heavy call/return patterns without compounding loop overhead. CorrectnessRisk weights stay modest for all passes: the workload is plain C++ with no exception-heavy or floating-point-sensitive code, so risk is low, but FLA/BCF/IBR retain slightly elevated risk weights so the selector avoids functions with complex CFGs or opaque predicates interacting with C++ object lifetime paths. IGV is included at moderate weight to obscure global state access, though this benchmark has few globals so its expected application is limited.
